newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Serbs block joint parliament session.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serbs block joint parliament session.

text.p: The first session of Bosnia's peacetime parliament has been postponed indefinitely because of Serb obstructiveness, diplomats said on Monday.
The session was delayed for three successive days and has been called off altogether due to Serb objections over the venue for government meetings.
"This is just pure obstruction," said one diplomat.
The parliament has never held a full session since Serb members boycotted an inaugural ceremony in October in Sarajevo, citing concerns over the text of an oath and the venue.
Now Bosnian Serb leaders are linking their parliamentary presence to objections over the venue for the newly-formed cabinet.

Despite an agreement to alternate cabinet meetings between the country's Moslem-Croat federation and its Serb republic, Bosnian Serbs wanted the council of ministers to meet more frequently on Serb territory.
The office of the international High Representative, which oversees the civilian aspects of the Bosnian peace deal, said the Serbs were reneging on a previous agreement.
Michael Steiner, deputy to the international High Representative, accused Serb leaders of blocking joint governing bodies meant to reunite the country after 3-1/2 years of war.
The German diplomat told reporters the Bosnian Serbs risked severe financial consequences by showing a reluctance to work within a peacetime government.

"This position...is quite irresponsible because in the end they will hurt their people, the population in the (Serb republic) who so urgently need economic and financial assistance which can only come via the common institutions."
Similar warnings in the past from the High Representative have failed to move the ultra-nationalist Serb leadership, which fought for a separate Serb state during 43 months of war.

The Dayton peace agreement obliges the Serbs to recognise a weak central government for Bosnia, comprised of a collective presidency and inter-ethnic parliament, ruling over Moslem-Croat and Serb territories.

The Bosnian Serbs receive a little reconstruction aid despite criticism of their refusal to extradite indicted war criminals, the blocking of refugees returning to Serb territory and their reluctance to work with joint governing bodies.
Serb deputies in the 42-member House of Representatives have yet to sign a solemn declaration upholding Bosnia's constitution and statehood, three months after post-war elections were held.
If the Serbs failed to compromise, the wartime Bosnian government would serve as a caretaker and represent Bosnia in talks with international financial institutions, Steiner added.
